## TL;DR

Addressed the third review pass for #1047 and synchronized the feature branch with main. The card and drawer now show check progress for persisted handoffs, ordinary active check runs, and locally held check slots. The progress bar stays indeterminate until a real percentage is available, and attempt/machine details appear when supplied. Table-driven UI coverage exercises indeterminate and determinate progress, an empty run list with a held slot, and a reload that hydrates a CLI-requested handoff without a live SSE event. The post-merge build, focused regressions, and final `repoos check --changed main` passed.

## Work and rationale

The repeated review finding was that the card’s progress element could exist in the template and still not read as a progress bar. Its shared `.check-progress` rules lived in `TaskDrawer.vue`’s scoped stylesheet. Vue scopes those rules to drawer elements, so they never applied to the separate `TaskCard.vue` component. The card therefore lacked the flex layout, progress width and accent styling used by the drawer. I moved those shared rules to the global UI stylesheet and kept the card-specific top spacing there as well. Both surfaces now use the same visible progress treatment.

The card previously rendered the progress row only when `handoffInFlight` was true. That omitted regular active check runs and a task holding a local check slot. I widened the condition to include all three ownership signals: server handoff status, any running task check, or a local slot held for the task. The progress object controls only the numeric value. A known percentage is rendered as determinate; absent or incomplete progress leaves the native `<progress>` value omitted, so it remains indeterminate rather than suggesting a fabricated percentage.

The card’s running hint now covers ordinary active check runs as well as handoff checks and local slots. It names the step and elapsed time. The status row uses the progress record’s machine and attempt where present, falling back to the persisted handoff snapshot. This keeps details visible after reload and when the check endpoint has no history row. The drawer uses the same source precedence. During the final regression run, an existing drawer test caught a generic heading that appended `step —` when no numbered progress existed; I removed that placeholder from the heading and kept “Starting…” in the progress detail row.

The new table-driven regression covers four data states: incomplete progress with server-supplied attempt and machine, determinate check-run progress (33%), a local slot held while the check list is empty, and a fresh component mount that receives running handoff status from `/handoff-status` with no SSE step. It checks both card and drawer progress values and metadata, plus suppression of the “Quiet — may be stalled” and “stuck · silent” warnings. The reload case verifies that the server status endpoint is actually requested.

The original investigation still explains the empty `runs` result: the handoff-status endpoint is the durable owner state, while check history is an optional run record and may not contain the CLI-started check. The UI now treats these sources as complementary instead of interpreting an empty run list as inactivity.

## Approaches tried

I read review passes 2 and 3 and the prior engineering report before syncing. `repoos sync 1047` refused because the CLI saw an engineer turn in progress, so I merged main directly in the task worktree. Git completed the merge without source conflicts; the earlier description of a conflict in `src/core/shot-fixtures.ts` was inaccurate. The merge brought in main’s then-current task bookkeeping, including its copy of the task work file. I rebuilt the application after the merge, then made the progress-bar and machine/attempt corrections on the resulting branch.

I first ran the new table-driven test and corrected two test/behavior issues it exposed: the drawer heading needed to prioritize persisted handoff stage over the generic running check step, and the reload test needed to verify the status API request rather than assume an EventSource instance is created in that test harness. Those focused cases passed. The first full changed-path gate then exposed the `step —` placeholder in an existing status-summary test. I removed the unknown progress detail from the heading, retained the dedicated “Starting…” detail, and reran the affected focused tests successfully.

## Challenges and blockers

The main-sync merge changed the base substantially. The UI change itself was narrower: shared progress styling had to be global to reach the card, while progress-state selection had to account for three distinct sources without changing the close-out stage’s priority. The screenshot fixture also needed to use the task ID already present in the declared drawer route; otherwise its synthetic task ID caused real API requests to return 404 during capture. A subsequent capture found that the drawer also fetched integration-conflict provenance for the fixture task. I added an ID-scoped capture guard for that server-backed read and a regression that confirms it is skipped only for the captured task while unrelated IDs and ordinary sessions still fetch normally.

The first final gate was not green: its broad test run reported two failing files, including a timing-sensitive `handoff-unification.test.ts` case that timed out while waiting for an earlier-turn marker to be ignored. A focused run of that file passed the case on retry, confirming timing sensitivity but exiting nonzero at the wrapper level. I therefore reran the full scoped gate on the unchanged tree. That final run passed remote build and tests, rendered contrast, UI smoke, and local formatting, lint, build, CSS/theme, hard-coded-color, and safety checks. The post-merge `bun run build` also succeeded. Focused verification passed the task card/drawer status tests and the shot fixture test. I opened the managed preview’s declared drawer state and visually confirmed the running step, determinate progress, attempt and machine; the automatic shot capture itself had previously been blocked by an in-flight capture lock.

## Key learnings

A visual component’s markup is not enough if its styling is scoped to a sibling component. Shared progress treatment belongs in global CSS when the same class is used by the card and teleported drawer. For live status, ownership and measurement are separate: handoff status or slot ownership establishes that checks are running, while progress data determines whether a bar can show a percentage.

The display should preserve the most specific known stage and omit placeholders when data is absent. “Starting…” is actionable and accurate; “step —” suggests a broken measurement. Finally, merge conflicts in fixtures and task bookkeeping need deliberate resolution: preserve feature and main fixture entries together, but keep the canonical main copy of the task work file when the workflow asks for it.
